opus-5.5.text:
I think "contempt" is maybe a strong word, but there's definitely a real tension, and I've lived on both sides of it, so I can understand where each camp is coming from.

From the traditional robotics side, the view is often: you learning people throw huge amounts of data and compute at a problem, you get a demo that works seventy percent of the time, you put it in a video with nice music, and you call it a breakthrough. But you can't tell me why it fails, you can't guarantee anything, and if I move the table two inches it falls apart. Meanwhile, we spent decades understanding dynamics, contact, control theory, and those tools actually give you reliability and interpretability. So there's a feeling that learning people are reinventing the wheel, badly, and ignoring hard-won knowledge.

From the learning side, the view is roughly the opposite: you classical people have been working on manipulation for forty years, and robots still can't fold laundry or load a dishwasher in a random home. Your methods work beautifully in structured settings, in factories, where you can model everything, but the real world is messy and you can't hand-write a model for every object and every situation. Look at what happened in vision and language: hand-engineered features lost to learning once data and compute scaled. Why would robotics be different?

Honestly, I think both critiques are partly right, and that's exactly why the tension exists. The classical folks are right that a lot of learning results are fragile, poorly evaluated, and hard to reproduce. The learning folks are right that the classical pipeline doesn't scale to open-world generality.

What I've come to believe is that the interesting work is in the middle. Things like having good low-level controllers, good state estimation, good hardware design, and then using learning for the parts that are genuinely hard to model, like perception, high-level decision making, dealing with deformable objects. Some of the most impressive systems I've seen, whether in locomotion or dexterous manipulation, quietly combine both: simulation built on real physics understanding, plus learned policies on top.

And there's a cultural dimension too. The two communities grew up with different values. Robotics people value rigor, systems that actually run on hardware, understanding failure modes. ML people value scale, generality, fast iteration, benchmarks. When you have different definitions of what "good research" looks like, it's very easy to look at the other side and think they're doing it wrong.

So I'd say the contempt mostly comes from each side seeing the other's weaknesses very clearly while underestimating its strengths. The people I respect most are the ones who can hold both views at once: who take data and scale seriously, but also know enough physics and control to understand when a robot is failing for reasons no amount of data will easily fix.

r001.rationale: The response describes each camp’s criticisms of the other and differing research values, but does not say that the mutual contempt reflects stronger belief in each camp’s own chosen approach.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "contempt" is a strong word, but there's definitely a real tension, and I've lived on both sides of it, so let me try to be fair.

The traditional robotics people, the control theory and planning folks, their whole discipline is built on guarantees. You write down a dynamics model, you prove stability, you can tell someone exactly when the system will fail. When they look at learning-based work, what they see is a lot of demos. A video of a robot folding a towel, trained on ten thousand trials, with no explanation of why it works, and no answer to the question "what happens if the towel is a different color." To them that feels unserious. It feels like you've replaced understanding with compute.

And the machine learning people look at classical robotics and see thirty years of beautiful theory that produced robots which still can't pick things up off a messy desk. Every method requires a hand-built model, every environment needs an engineer to re-tune it, and the moment the world deviates from the assumptions, the whole thing breaks. So from their side, the rigor looks like rigor about the wrong problem.

What I've come to believe is that both groups are actually reacting to the same thing, which is that the real world is extremely unforgiving, and each side has a different strategy for coping with it. One side tries to constrain the problem until it's provable. The other side tries to throw enough data at it that the mess gets absorbed. Neither one is complete.

The strongest people I know don't really pick a camp. If you talk to someone who has actually shipped a robot into a factory or a home, they'll tell you the learned policy is wrapped in a classical safety controller, and the planner uses a learned perception module, and nobody feels embarrassed about that. The contempt mostly lives in paper reviews and on Twitter. It lives much less in deployment, because deployment humbles everyone.

I'd also say the tension is partly generational and partly institutional. The classical crowd built their careers on expertise that is now partly being commoditized by data, and that's a genuinely uncomfortable position to be in. And the ML crowd is often young and hasn't yet been burned by a robot that worked perfectly in simulation and then hurt someone's hand. Some of the mutual disdain is really just people at different stages of being humbled.

So my honest take is that the contempt is a symptom of a field that hasn't converged yet. When robotics finally has its equivalent of the transformer moment, where one approach clearly works and everyone adopts it, I think the argument will dissolve, and we'll look back and find it a bit silly that we spent so much energy on it.

r001.rationale: The response explains that each group views the other’s approach as inadequate: traditional robotics researchers value guarantees, while ML researchers see classical methods as brittle. This conveys mutual contempt rooted in confidence in their chosen approaches.

astra-6.text:
I think some of that contempt comes from different ideas about what counts as solving a problem. A traditional robotics researcher might ask: Can you explain why the system works? Can you characterize its stability and predict when it will fail? A machine learning researcher might ask: Can it learn a behavior we don’t know how to program, and can it improve as we give it more data?

Those are both legitimate questions. But each side can mistake the other side’s priorities for a lack of rigor. One sees a learned policy and says, “That’s a black box.” The other sees a carefully engineered controller and says, “That only works because you designed everything around this particular task.” Sometimes those criticisms are fair. They become less useful when they turn into judgments about an entire field.

Robotics makes that division especially awkward because you have to deal with the physical world. Learning doesn’t make dynamics, latency, or safety constraints disappear. At the same time, a good dynamics model doesn’t automatically tell a robot how to handle the variety of objects and situations it will encounter.

So I’d rather ask where each method earns its place. What should we model explicitly? What should we learn? How do we detect and recover from failure? Once you’re responsible for making the whole robot work, there’s a strong incentive to care less about which camp a method belongs to.

r001.rationale: The response attributes contempt to different ideas of what counts as solving a problem and each side misreading the other’s priorities. It does not clearly say that researchers hold stronger belief in the approach they chose.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of that contempt comes from people having different ideas about what counts as progress. If you work in machine learning, you may look at a robotics system with lots of carefully designed modules and say, “How much of this can really generalize?” If you work in traditional robotics, you may look at a learned policy and say, “You have an impressive demonstration, but do you understand when it will fail?” Both questions are legitimate. The contempt starts when people assume that because the other approach doesn’t answer their favorite question, it has no value.

Robotics makes this especially visible because the physical world is unforgiving. Learning offers a way to deal with things that are difficult to model explicitly. Traditional methods give us structure, constraints, and ways to reason about behavior. Neither advantage makes the other irrelevant.

So I would bring the discussion back to a concrete task: What does the robot need to do? Under what conditions? How reliably? With how much data and engineering effort? Once you agree on those things, you can compare approaches meaningfully—and often you discover that the useful system combines them. The goal is to make the robot work, not to prove that your research community was right all along.

r001.rationale: The response describes different standards for progress and critiques each approach’s limitations, but does not say researchers’ contempt reflects stronger belief in the approach they chose.
